title: Zoom Levels
summary: Tablewise's booking system seen twice: as a high-level service map, then from inside one service, with its API, data model and classes.

goals.text: Say what a high-level design must show, and what it leaves out
Zoom into one service: modules, API contract and data model
Use the low-level design to enforce a rule the map can't
Move between both levels in a design interview

steps.title: Tablewise, from 10,000 feet
body: Tablewise lets diners book tables at 3,000 restaurants. This is its high-level design (HLD): a gateway, two services, their databases, and an event stream that a notifier reads to send confirmations.
Each box is something you deploy and own. Each arrow is a network call or a message. Nothing here says how a booking actually works inside.

steps.title: What the map is for
body: An HLD answers system-wide questions: what are the parts, who calls whom, which calls are synchronous and which are async events, where data lives, and what scales or fails independently.
It deliberately hides everything inside a box. That is what makes it useful for talking about the whole system at once, with a team or in an interview.
changes: + Panel: what a high-level design answers

card.title: What the map answers
lines: which **services** exist and who owns them
how they talk: **sync** calls vs **async** events
what scales out, and what fails alone
# no classes, no columns, no code

steps.title: Two diners, one table
body: Ana and Raj both tap 8 pm, table 4 within the same second. Both requests reach the Booking service. Do both get a confirmation?

The map can't answer. The arrow from the Booking service to its database looks exactly the same whether the code checks then inserts (racy) or relies on the database to refuse a duplicate (safe). The answer lives one zoom level down.

callout.text: Many real bugs hide inside a single box: races, missing idempotency, a wrong index. A service map can't show any of them.

changes: + Ana and Raj book the same table

steps.title: Open up one box
body: Low-level design (LLD) zooms into one service. Its parts are now modules and classes: a controller that speaks HTTP, the booking logic, an availability check, a repository that talks to the database, and an event publisher.
The other services drop out of view. They still exist, but at this zoom level they are just the outside world.
changes: - Restaurant service, Notifier, their stores (out of frame)
~ Bookings DB moves below the repository

steps.title: Pin down the API
body: The first LLD artifact is the contract: endpoints, request fields and every response the caller must handle. Note the idempotency_key, so a retry after a timeout can't create a second booking, and the explicit 409 Conflict for a slot that is already gone.
Writing errors down at this level forces the hard decisions early. What should Raj see? Here, the next free slot.

steps.title: Design the tables
body: Next, the data model. A reservations row ties a table to a time slot, and a unique constraint on (table_id, slot) makes a double booking impossible, no matter how the application code is scheduled.
An index on (restaurant_id, slot) keeps the availability query fast, and a small idempotency table maps each key to the reservation it already created.

card.title: Data model
lines: = one table + one slot = at most one row

steps.title: The database says no
body: Replay the race. Both requests pass the availability check, because it ran before either insert. Ana's INSERT commits first; Raj's breaks the unique constraint, the repository turns that into a SlotTaken error, and the controller returns 409 with the 8:30 alternative.
No locks held across network calls, no distributed coordination. One constraint, chosen at the LLD level, closes the race the HLD couldn't even show.

callout.text: Treat the availability check as a hint for the UI. The constraint is the real guarantee.

changes: ~ Insert labelled on the repository link

steps.title: Dependencies point inward
body: Inside the service, the booking logic depends only on small interfaces it defines: ReservationStore, EventSink, AvailabilityPolicy. The Postgres and Kafka code implement those interfaces at the edges.
That's why the core can be unit-tested with in-memory fakes, and why swapping the message broker later touches one adapter, not the business rules.
changes: ~ Booking logic now depends only on interfaces

card.title: Dependencies point inward
lines: = tests swap adapters for in-memory fakes

steps.title: Back to the map, better informed
body: Zoom back out. The service map barely changed, but now two notes on it carry real weight: bookings return 409 on conflict, and the database enforces one row per table and slot.

Some LLD choices push back up. That constraint only works if all bookings for a table live in one database, which rules out splitting a restaurant's tables across shards. The levels inform each other.

callout.text: In an interview: sketch the whole map first, then say “let me zoom into the booking path”. Pick one or two boxes; never all of them.

changes: + Restaurant service, Notifier, stores back in view
~ Booking service annotated with the LLD decisions

steps.title: Two zoom levels, one system
body:
• HLD: services, stores, queues and the calls between them. Answers scale, ownership and failure questions.
  • LLD: inside one service. Modules, API contract, data model, classes.
  • Races, idempotency and indexes are LLD problems; you can't see them on the map.
  • Keep the core logic free of I/O and depend on interfaces you own.
  • LLD decisions can constrain the HLD (for example, what can be sharded).
  • In interviews, go wide first, then deep on one or two boxes.
